title: Searching Maryland Unclaimed Property for a Loved One (November 2026)
summary: A November 2026 guide to Maryland unclaimed property for deceased owners, covering eligibility, claims, and required documents.
body_markdown:
In Maryland, money and financial assets left inactive long enough are reported to the state as unclaimed property, which can include a deceased person’s bank accounts, uncashed checks, and insurance payments. Whether the state holds any of a loved one’s property depends on how long an account or payment was inactive, not on the date of death. This guide explains key points for families and executors to be aware of, including: how Maryland unclaimed property works, how to search claimitmd.gov, who is authorized to claim for a deceased owner, what documents a claim requires, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- Claimitmd.gov offers free searches using the deceased person's name.
- Claims for deceased owners usually require court-issued authority, not a will alone.
- Maryland claim status is available online through KAPS after login.
- State unclaimed property searches exclude active accounts and in-force life insurance.
- Elayne requests roughly 10 years of IRS tax transcripts with authorization to identify asset leads.


## What Maryland Unclaimed Property Is


Maryland unclaimed property includes money and financial assets left inactive long enough that businesses must report them to the state. These records can help families[find forgotten checking accounts](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-find-assets-deceased-person) , uncashed checks, or insurance payments left behind by a deceased person.


The Maryland unclaimed property FAQ lists:


- Checking and savings accounts, including certificates of deposit
- Uncashed checks, including payroll checks
- Insurance payments
- Dividends, stocks, and bonds
- Safe deposit box contents with monetary value


Real estate, vehicles, and boats are excluded. A search is not a full inventory of the person's belongings.

## When Property Becomes Unclaimed in Maryland


Maryland’s unclaimed property reporting clock generally starts with inactivity, not the owner’s death. The[state’s general FAQ](https://www.claimitmd.gov/app/faq-general) specifies the reporting periods below:


Property type When reporting is required


Most financial accounts and uncashed checks After three years of inactivity


Nursing home accounts After one year


Uncashed travelers’ checks 15 years after issue


Institutions then report and remit funds to the Comptroller’s Office. Its[unclaimed property service notice](https://www.marylandcomptroller.gov/content/dam/mdcomp/md/media/2026/01-30-2026-comptroller-governor-urge-marylanders-to-search-for-their-unclaimed-property.pdf) explains the general three-year rule.


## How Maryland Holds and Safeguards the Funds


Maryland holds unclaimed property indefinitely under a custodial system. Under this system, the state holds it for the rightful owner without ending the owner’s right to claim it. That right continues after death: legitimate heirs can claim the property.


The Comptroller’s Office also works to locate owners through newspaper notices, mailed postcards, and community outreach.


In October 2025, the Comptroller launched its new system, the Kelmar Abandoned Property System (KAPS). It introduced online claims, electronic document submission, and claim status tracking, allowing families to submit paperwork and follow the status of an unclaimed property claim online.


## How to Search for a Deceased Person's Unclaimed Property in Maryland


The[Maryland Comptroller's unclaimed property site](https://www.claimitmd.gov/) offers a free search without an account. Searches use the deceased person's first and last name.


The name used is the person's own name, not “Estate of.” Results show matching property records held by the Maryland Comptroller. A matching name is a lead to review as part of an[unclaimed inheritance search](https://www.elayne.com/resources/unclaimed-property-and-inheritance-search-guide) , not proof that the funds belong to the loved one.


If no results appear, searching former names or alternate spellings can help account for differences in records.


## Who Is Authorized to Claim on Behalf of a Deceased Owner


Being named in a will alone does not authorize someone to claim Maryland unclaimed property for a deceased owner. In most cases, court-issued authority is required.


The claim route depends on the estate’s status:


- A court-appointed representative uses letters of administration with Claim Form ST912 or the online claim.
- A small estate affidavit may support a claim where Maryland’s requirements allow it.


Without court papers, the Comptroller must confirm the accepted alternative route and required proof before a relative files a claim. Kinship alone does not prove entitlement.


## What Documentation Maryland Requires to File a Claim


A Maryland unclaimed property claim for a deceased owner typically requires:


- Completed Claim Form ST912 or its online equivalent.
- A copy of the owner’s death certificate.
- Letters of administration or other accepted proof of legal authority.
- A copy of the claimant’s identification.


The claim instructions specify any further evidence needed.


## Searching Beyond Maryland: Nearby States and Federal Sources


Unclaimed property generally follows the owner’s last known location in the holder’s records, not necessarily where they lived at death. Searches can include states where the person lived or did business, such as Virginia and New York.


[MissingMoney's free multistate search](https://missingmoney.com/) covers participating states. Federal unclaimed funds require separate searches.


## What Unclaimed Property Searches Do Not Cover


State unclaimed property databases contain only property already turned over to the state. They exclude accounts and policies still active, including current retirement accounts and in-force life insurance, which calls for a separate[decedent's life insurance search](https://www.elayne.com/resources/decedent-life-insurance-search-guide) .


A search with no matches does not rule out other assets. Families can continue searching through individual state programs and financial institutions named in their loved one's statements or mail.

## How Elayne Supports Families Searching a Deceased Loved One's Accounts


Elayne Asset Search is a service that helps families[find bank and investment accounts after death](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-find-all-bank-and-investment-accounts-after-someone-dies) , along with property and debts of a person who died. Search results are organized into a single estate inventory, and each finding shows where the information came from.


### What an IRS tax transcript shows


Elayne holds IRS authorization to request roughly 10 years of IRS tax transcripts for the person who died. An IRS tax transcript is not a tax return. A transcript lists what banks, employers, insurers, and other institutions reported to the IRS about the person.


Each institution on a transcript points to a financial relationship, such as a bank account, a brokerage account, an insurance policy, or a retirement account. Elayne also requests the person's Equifax credit report, which lists open accounts, credit cards, and debts in the person's name.


A state search such as claimitmd.gov matches property already turned over to that state. IRS tax transcripts and credit reports can point to accounts still held by a bank or insurer.


### Other sources in the same search


The search also checks more than 100 other sources, including:


- Life insurance locators for in-force and lapsed policies
- The federal pension registry, which lists unclaimed pensions from terminated plans
- The national unclaimed property database, which covers property turned over to participating states
- Property and vehicle records
- Crypto accounts, when transcripts or other estate records point to crypto
- Veterans benefits and VA life insurance, when records show veteran status


Debts appear alongside assets, so the inventory shows what the estate owes as well as what the person owned.


In practice, the search turns institution names from transcripts and credit reports into a documented list of leads, each tied to a named source.


## FAQ


### Is a three-year wait required before searching claimitmd.gov after a loved one dies?


No, families can search immediately because Maryland may already hold money from accounts that became inactive before the death. The reporting period starts with inactivity, not death; accounts still held by a bank require follow-up with that institution.


### How do MissingMoney and the NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator differ when a loved one may have had insurance?


The tools cover different stages: MissingMoney searches property turned over to participating states, while the NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator helps trace policies through insurers. If an insurance payment never reached the loved one, state searches may help; if a policy may have existed, the NAIC locator provides a separate search route.


### How can families confirm that a claimitmd.gov result belongs to their loved one when the name is common?


Families can compare the reporting company and any identifying details in the result with their loved one’s statements, mail, and other records. If the connection remains unclear, Maryland’s Unclaimed Property Division can explain what evidence is needed before a claim is submitted; a matching name alone does not prove ownership.


### Is there a deadline to claim Maryland unclaimed property for a deceased owner?


No. Maryland holds unclaimed property indefinitely under a custodial system, which means the state keeps the property for the rightful owner without ending the owner’s right to claim. That right continues after death, and legitimate heirs can claim the property. There is no statute of limitations on claiming.


### What kinds of property can appear in a Maryland unclaimed property search?


Maryland’s unclaimed property FAQ lists checking and savings accounts (including certificates of deposit), uncashed checks (including payroll checks), insurance payments, dividends, stocks, bonds, and safe deposit box contents with monetary value. Real estate, vehicles, and boats are excluded. A search result is not a full inventory of a person’s belongings.


### Does searching claimitmd.gov require an account, and which name is used?


The Maryland Comptroller’s search is free and does not require an account. Searches use the deceased person’s own first and last name, not “Estate of.” Searching former names or alternate spellings can account for differences in how records were entered.
